summary: Defines an SMTP service extension that lets a client indicate an authentication mechanism to the server, run an authentication exchange, and optionally negotiate a security layer for later traffic. It was replaced by RFC 4954.

eli5.summary: This lets a mail program prove who it is, with a password for example, before the mail server agrees to send its mail.

questions: how do mail clients log in to smtp
what is the auth parameter to mail from
subtitle: Letting mail clients prove their identity to the mail server before sending mail.

tldr.problem: SMTP as originally defined allowed anyone to connect and send mail, with no way for a server to verify who is sending. Mail clients and submission agents needed a standard way to authenticate.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2554 adds an AUTH command to SMTP that lets a client indicate a SASL authentication mechanism, perform an authentication exchange, and optionally negotiate a security layer (encryption) for subsequent commands.
tldr.outcome: SMTP AUTH became the standard way for mail clients to authenticate to mail servers. It was superseded by RFC 4954, which clarified and extended the mechanism.

today: RFC 2554 is obsoleted by RFC 4954. However, SMTP AUTH itself remains the standard way for mail clients to authenticate to mail servers. Most mail servers and clients support it, and it is mandatory for mail submission (RFC 2476).

sections.title: The Problem and the Solution
sections.content:
Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) was designed to be a simple protocol for sending mail between systems on a trusted network. It includes no authentication: any client that connects can claim to be anyone and send mail on their behalf. This worked when the Internet was small and trusted, but it enabled spam and spoofing.

RFC 2554 adds an authentication mechanism to SMTP using the Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL), a framework for pluggable authentication mechanisms. A mail client can now connect to a server and prove its identity using a mechanism that both sides support—such as login with a password, a challenge-response hash, or even Kerberos.

The extension also allows negotiation of a security layer (typically TLS encryption) for the rest of the session, protecting the subsequent mail commands from snooping.
sections.eli5: Before, anyone could pretend to be you when sending mail to a server. Now the server can ask 'who are you?' and the client can prove it by using a password or other proof.

sections.title: The AUTH Command
sections.content:
A client initiates authentication with the AUTH command, specifying a SASL mechanism (such as PLAIN, LOGIN, CRAM-MD5, or DIGEST-MD5) and optionally including an initial response. The syntax is AUTH mechanism [initial-response].

If the server recognizes the mechanism, it sends a 334 challenge (a BASE64-encoded string). The client responds with a BASE64-encoded answer. The server may send more challenges; the client answers each one. If at any point the client wants to cancel, it sends a single asterisk. If the authentication succeeds, the server sends a 235 reply. If it fails, the server sends a 535 reply (or a more specific error code).

Once authentication succeeds, no further AUTH commands are allowed in that session. The authenticated identity is available for subsequent commands, such as the MAIL FROM command, which can declare on whose behalf the message is being sent.
sections.eli5: The client says 'I want to use CRAM-MD5.' The server sends a challenge. The client sends an answer. If the answer is right, the server says 'OK, it's you.'

sections.title: Choosing an Authentication Mechanism
sections.content:
After a client connects with EHLO (Extended HELO), the server advertises which SASL mechanisms it supports using the AUTH keyword in its response. The client then chooses one mechanism and issues an AUTH command with that mechanism name.

If the server does not support the requested mechanism, it replies with a 504 error. The client may then try a different mechanism by issuing another AUTH command, unless authentication has already succeeded.

The initial-response parameter allows optimization: some SASL mechanisms (like PLAIN) send no data in the server's first challenge, expecting the client to send all credentials in response to an empty challenge. By including the initial-response in the AUTH command itself, the client saves a round trip.
sections.eli5: The server says 'I support CRAM-MD5 and PLAIN.' The client picks one and tries it. If the server doesn't support it, the client can try another.

sections.title: Optional Encryption After Authentication
sections.content:
Some SASL mechanisms can negotiate a security layer—typically TLS-style encryption—that protects all subsequent commands from that point forward. After the successful 235 response, the security layer takes effect immediately, and the SMTP conversation resets to its initial state.

Both client and server must discard any state they learned before authentication (such as the list of SMTP extensions) because an attacker could have modified it. After the security layer is active, the client should send a new EHLO command to learn the server's capabilities over the encrypted channel.

This provides confidentiality and integrity for sensitive commands like MAIL FROM and message data, protecting them from network sniffing or tampering.
sections.eli5: After proving who you are, you can also agree to lock the door so no one else can read your mail orders. The server forgets everything it heard before the lock, so an attacker can't trick it.

sections.title: Tracking Message Origin in Relays
sections.content:
RFC 2554 adds an optional AUTH parameter to the MAIL FROM command. When a client sends a message on behalf of a user, it can include AUTH=user@example.com to assert who originally submitted the message.

If the server trusts the authenticated identity of the client, and the client is claiming the message came from a particular user, the server may include the same AUTH parameter when relaying the message to another server. This creates a chain of trust: downstream servers can verify that the message was authenticated at an earlier hop.

If the client is not authenticated, or if the server does not trust the client to assert message origin, the server uses AUTH=<> (empty brackets), meaning the original submitter is unknown or not authenticated. This prevents a malicious or compromised client from forging the appearance of an authenticated origin.
sections.eli5: When a mail relay passes a message to another server, it can say 'the original sender proved they are alice@example.com.' Downstream servers can trust this if they trust the relay.

sections.title: Error Codes and Security Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 2554 defines several error codes for specific authentication failures. A 432 reply means the user must first authenticate using the PLAIN mechanism (password transition). A 534 reply indicates the chosen mechanism is too weak for that user or server policy. A 538 reply means the mechanism requires encryption (TLS) to be enabled first.

Security is critical: before SASL negotiation begins, protocol interactions are unencrypted and can be modified by an attacker. Clients and servers must discard any unencrypted knowledge obtained before authentication, especially if a security layer is negotiated afterward. A client requiring secure submission should be configured to never send mail to a server unless the connection is both authenticated and encrypted.

The extension is not a replacement for end-to-end message signing or encryption (like S/MIME or PGP). It protects the transaction with the server but not the message content itself after delivery.
sections.eli5: If something goes wrong during login—the password is weak, or the connection isn't encrypted enough—the server sends a specific error so the client knows what to fix.
